summary_html: Agency makes a **substantiated (founded)** finding of abuse/neglect. This decision often unlocks **court petitions**, **service mandates**, and **federal reporting** duties.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — definitions floor; data & record requirements  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — outcomes & safety performance reviews

primary_citations.citation_text: New York - N.Y. Soc. Serv. Law § 411 et seq. (Child Protective Services Act – reporting requirements)
New York - Family Court Act Article 10 (Abuse/Neglect juvenile proceedings)

New York - N.Y. Soc. Serv. Law § 422 (Statewide Central Register; for investigations commenced on or after January 1, 2022 a report is indicated only where there is a fair preponderance of the evidence that the alleged abuse or maltreatment occurred, and the burden of proof at the subject's fair hearing is on the child protective service which investigated the report)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Matter of Lee TT. v. Dowling
key_cases.holding: The Court of Appeals held that the 'some credible evidence' standard for retaining an indicated report in the Statewide Central Register violates federal due process to the extent the report is disseminated to provider and licensing agencies, and that a subject is entitled to a pre-deprivation hearing at which the agency must prove the abuse or maltreatment by a fair preponderance of the evidence.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading New York authority on the evidentiary standard and hearing rights attaching to a substantiated (indicated) finding.
key_cases.quote: subjects are entitled to a predeprivation hearing to determine by a fair preponderance of the evidence whether reports of abuse can be substantiated and relevant to future employment or licensure

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed confirmation of an indicated Central Register report, holding that there is no constitutional right to assigned counsel at a Statewide Central Register administrative fair hearing and that the 2020 amendments to Social Services Law § 422 - including the fair-preponderance standard and the irrebuttable presumption from an article 10 dismissal - do not apply retroactively to determinations rendered before their January 1, 2022 effective date.
key_cases.relevance: This is the current Court of Appeals decision on the procedural protections and evidentiary standard governing a substantiated finding.
key_cases.quote: Inclusion on the SCR—unlike Family Court article 10 proceedings—does not impact rights that we have concluded warrant recognition of a constitutional right to assigned counsel in civil proceedings

key_cases.case_name: Matter of Elizabeth B. v. New York State Office of Children & Family Services
key_cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Third Department
key_cases.holding: The Third Department annulled the portion of the OCFS determination that maintained an indicated report of inadequate guardianship against a mother who was herself the victim of domestic violence, ordering the report unfounded, expunged and sealed, because the minimum-degree-of-care inquiry must account for the risks and constraints she actually faced.
key_cases.relevance: It applies the fair-preponderance maltreatment standard and Nicholson's minimum-degree-of-care test to an administrative substantiation.
key_cases.quote: Respondent misconstrues this standard as one that cannot be "modified or excused because a parent is under stress or fear."

key_cases.holding: Affirming findings of abuse and an order of supervision, the Court held that Family Court Act § 1046(a)(ii) creates only a rebuttable presumption shifting the burden of going forward to the respondents, while the burden of proving abuse by a preponderance always remains with the petitioning agency.
key_cases.relevance: It fixes the burden of proof and the evidentiary weight of a res ipsa-style prima facie case behind a founded finding.
key_cases.quote: The establishment of a prima facie case does not require the court to find that the parents were culpable; it merely establishes a rebuttable presumption of parental culpability

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed abuse findings in two proceedings, holding that as amended Family Court Act § 1046(a)(vi) permits a child's out-of-court statements to be corroborated by any other evidence tending to support their reliability, including validation testimony by a qualified expert and the cross-corroborating statements of other child victims.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling New York rule on the corroboration required before a child's hearsay disclosure can support a founded finding.
key_cases.quote: As amended, section 1046 (a) (vi) states a broad flexible rule providing that out-of-court statements may be corroborated by "[a]ny other evidence tending to support" their reliability

key_cases.case_name: Matter of Nassau County Dep't of Social Servs. ex rel. Dante M. v. Denise J.
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a newborn's positive toxicology for a controlled substance cannot by itself support a neglect finding because it does not establish the causative connection to actual or imminent impairment that Family Court Act § 1012(f)(i)(B) requires, but affirmed the findings and the one-year order of supervision because other evidence - prematurity, low birth weight, intensive-care and high-risk follow-up needs, and the mother's cocaine use during pregnancy - showed imminent danger of impairment to both children.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading New York causation authority for a founded finding: the agency must link the medical result to actual or imminent impairment rather than treat the result itself as the finding.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that more than a positive toxicology is generally required for a neglect determination.

statutory_basis.citation_text: N.Y. Soc. Serv. Law § 422(5)(a), (8)(b)(ii) (fair preponderance of the evidence standard for investigations commenced on or after January 1, 2022; the burden of proof in the subject's fair hearing is on the child protective service which investigated the report)

timeline_requirements.starts_from: Receipt of the report (the investigation or family assessment response itself must commence within 24 hours)
A determination that the investigation did not find a fair preponderance of the evidence that the alleged abuse or maltreatment occurred (investigations commenced on or after January 1, 2022)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in N.Y. Soc. Serv. Law § 422(5)

timeline_requirements.requirement_name: Request to amend an indicated report
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Notice to the subject of the report that the report is indicated
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in N.Y. Soc. Serv. Law § 422(8)(a)

notice_requirements.timing: In writing, no later than 7 days after receipt of the oral report
content_required: Rights of the subject of the report

statutory_basis.citation_text: 18 NYCRR 432.2(b)(3)(ii)(f) (after seeing that the children named in the report are safe, the child protective service must notify the subjects and other persons named in the report, in writing, no later than seven days after receipt of the oral report, of the existence of the report and the subject's rights)
